title: Execution Trace Cache vs. Conventional Instruction L1 Cache
where_in_paper: Trace Cache / Instruction Fetch and Decode
decision: Remove the conventional instruction L1 cache from the main pipeline and replace it with an Execution Trace Cache that caches decoded x86 micro-ops (uops) in their dynamically executed path order.
alternatives_or_rejected: Traditional instruction L1 cache that stores raw x86 instruction bytes requiring fetch-time instruction decoding and alignment every cycle.
rationale: x86 instructions are variable length and complex to decode; decoding them at high target clock frequencies would require excessive pipeline stages and power. Storing already-decoded uops eliminates decode latency/power on cache hits and delivers high uop bandwidth even across target branches.
outcome: Delivered a high-bandwidth uop stream (up to 3 uops per cycle) directly to the execution engine while bypassing x86 instruction decoding during normal loop/trace execution.
weakest_point: Exact section heading name used for the Trace Cache discussion

title: Double-Pumped Fast ALU Execution Engine
decision: Run core integer ALUs at twice the main core processor clock frequency (e.g. 2x clock speed), enabling simple ALU operations to complete in half a main clock cycle.
alternatives_or_rejected: Standard single-frequency ALUs executing one operation per main clock cycle.
rationale: High-frequency clock targets make latency (in clock cycles) for simple integer operations critical to dependent instruction chains; double-pumping the ALUs cuts dependent integer latency in half and effectively doubles integer throughput per unit area.
outcome: Achieved sub-nanosecond integer execution latency for low-latency operations like addition and subtraction.
weakest_point: Whether specific double-pumped ALU circuit schematics were detailed in this specific ITJ overview paper

title: Deep Pipeline Strategy for High Frequency (Hyper Pipelining)
decision: Implement a deep 20-stage branch misprediction penalty pipeline (Hyper Pipelining) to drastically reduce logic gate delays per stage.
rationale: Reducing logic levels per clock stage allows scaling the processor to significantly higher operational clock frequencies in a given process node, yielding overall higher performance despite higher branch mispredict penalties.
outcome: Enabled gigahertz-plus clock frequencies far exceeding previous generation P6 processors.
weakest_point: Exact wording used to introduce the 20-stage count figure in the text

title: Advanced Branch Prediction Engine Architecture
decision: Implement a large branch target buffer (BTB) combined with an advanced dynamic branch prediction algorithm incorporating both global and local history to drive the trace cache.
alternatives_or_rejected: Basic static branch prediction or smaller P6-style branch target buffers.
rationale: Because the deep 20-stage pipeline imposes a severe clock-cycle penalty on branch mispredictions, prediction accuracy had to be significantly higher than prior microarchitectures to maintain net IPC.
outcome: Reduced branch misprediction frequency significantly relative to older processors, protecting deep pipeline throughput.
weakest_point: Specific software benchmark misprediction reduction percentages quoted in text

title: Point-to-Point 400 MHz Quad-Pumped System Bus
decision: Utilize a 100 MHz physical system bus clock that is quad-pumped (4x data transfer per cycle) to provide 400 MHz equivalent data transfer rate (3.2 GB/s bandwidth).
alternatives_or_rejected: Single- or dual-data-rate system buses bounded by the physical clock frequency.
rationale: The high-frequency execution core and trace cache demand immense memory bandwidth to prevent stall states, which traditional bus clocking schemes could not supply within system board noise/electrical constraints.
outcome: Delivered up to 3.2 GB/s of system interconnect bandwidth to support streaming applications and high-speed memory.
weakest_point: Exact figure numbers for the system bus timing diagram in the paper
